name: Starter: Latin
about: Classical Latin in real, everyday sentences, with each one's words in Latin order and their long vowels marked until you know them.

words.ego: I (mihi: to me; mecum: with me)
words.in: in, on (with where); into (with where to)
words.ago: do, drive (quid agis?: how are you?; gratias ago: I thank)

items.text: Theam unam et aquam unam, quaeso.
items.means: A tea and a water, please.
wrong: Theam unum et aquam unam, quaeso.
Theam unam et aquam unum, quaeso.
Ego bene es, gratias tibi ago.
Ego bene est, gratias tibi ago.

items.means: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
I live in a small house.
Excuse me, where is the station?
My mother goes to the city.
Tomorrow I go to the city.

items.text: Gratias tibi ago. Cras te videbo!
wrong: Gratias tibi ago. Cras tu videbo!
Gratias tibi ago. Cras tibi videbo!

items.means: My mother works in the city.
I have a brother and a sister.

items.text: Frater meus linguam Latinam non intellegit.
wrong: Frater meus linguam Latinam non intellego.

items.means: The boys are playing in the garden.
The girl's book is on the table.
The cat is sleeping on the table.
The girl is writing a letter.
We had dinner at an inn yesterday.
I'm waiting for a friend in the forum.

concept.line: A verb's ending says who does it, so ego (I) and tu (you) are usually left out: amo (I love), amas (you love), amat (he or she loves), amamus (we love).
sum (I am), es (you are), est (is), sumus (we are), estis (you all are), sunt (they are); est usually comes last: Domus nostra magna est (house our big is).

words.means: es = you are; esne = are you?

concept.line: A describing word takes its noun's gender, number and case: domus magna (house big), cibus bonus (food good), clavis mea (key my); with no person or thing named, it's neuter: frigidum est (cold it-is: it's cold).

words.means: habeo = I have; habesne = do you have?

concept.line: A question word usually comes first (Ubi habitas?

words.means: loquerisne = do you speak?; loquor = I speak
intellego = I understand; intellegit = understands; intellegisne = do you understand?

concept.line: What a verb acts on takes its object form, often ending in -m: puella → puellam, frater → fratrem, liber → librum (Librum lego: book I-read).

words.means: habitat = lives; habito = I live; habitas = you live
vadis = you go; vado = I go; vadit = goes

concept.line: Where you're going takes the accusative: in urbem (into the city), and a city's name alone with no in: Romam (to Rome).

words.means: laboro = I work; laborare = to work; laborat = works; laborabo = I will work
